title: One year after shooting death, Bhutanese family still asking 'Why?'
article: A death still fresh on the Puri's minds, the loss of their son stings a year later.
"We came to Canada for peace," they said through a Nepali translator. "Our son was going to take care of us, but police killed him."
In July 2012, officers were called to a late-night disturbance. The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) determined the family was cleared out.
Less than two minutes later, a pair of constables fatally shot a knife-wielding Deu Raj Puri.
The officers have been cleared of wrong-doing in the case, but for Bhutanese refugees who had only settled in Lethbridge eight months prior, it's difficult to understand why.
"I was not satisfied with the result," said Naress Puri, Deu Raj's brother.
The Puris had called police that evening, reporting Deu Raj had a knife, was cutting himself, and threatening others.
Now, after losing one of their own, many of Lethbridge's 700 Bhutanese residents are thinking twice about calling law enforcement.
"They had placed the authorities (on a high pedestal)," said Hemlal Timsina, Canadian Bhutanese Society president. "They've lost that trust."
"They'd rather run away than deal with it."
Investigators acknowledged a language barrier helped escalate tensions that night.

"I don't pretend to know what it would be like living 20 years in a refugee camp in Nepal," Clif Purvis, ASIRT executive director, said Thursday. "Obviously he had difficulties you and I will never know about."
Despite trouble with alcohol, Naress Puri said Deu Raj was doing his best to learn English and fit in to Canada.
"We used to live for 18 years in the same house," he said. "(It feels like) something is missing."
